_meta.description: Reference cost, land-use, fuel-price and deflator values used by workstream C (Evaluate). Each entry uses the common shape {value, units, kind, source, url, note, retrieved, verified, verification_note}. Unit constants: 1 mile = 1.609344 km (exact); 1 hectare = 2.4710538 acres. Transmission and substation values keep the dollar year of their cost guide (stated in each note); nothing here is deflated except where a note says so. Raw source downloads are in data/evaluate/raw/costs/ (git-ignored). Gas prices are reproduced by `cd backend && .venv/bin/python -m app.evaluate.prep_gas`. Independently verified 2026-10-23 against the cited sources (see each entry's verification_note); verifier downloads are in data/evaluate/raw/costs_verify/ (git-ignored).

deflator_2023_to_2024.source: U.S. BLS, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), U.S. city average, All items, not seasonally adjusted, series CUUR0000SA0, annual averages
deflator_2023_to_2024.note: BLS API rows (period M13 = 'Annual'): 2024 annual = 313.689, 2023 annual = 304.702 (1982-84 = 100). Ratio 313.689 / 304.702 = 1.029494. Multiply 2023 USD by this to get 2024 USD. For a 2025-USD source (such as the 2025 PTO cost guides below), the same API gives 2025 annual = 321.943, so 2025 -> 2024 is 313.689 / 321.943 = 0.974362.

deflator_2025_to_2024.source: U.S. BLS, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), U.S. city average, All items, not seasonally adjusted, series CUUR0000SA0, annual averages
deflator_2025_to_2024.note: BLS API rows (period M13 = 'Annual'), the same facts as deflator_2023_to_2024's note: 2024 annual = 313.689, 2025 annual = 321.943 (1982-84 = 100). Ratio 313.689 / 321.943 = 0.974362. Multiply 2025 USD by this to get 2024 USD. Griddy applies it to the 2025 PG&E and SCE generator interconnection unit cost guides (transmission_line_*_usd_per_km and substation_*_usd) in backend/app/evaluate/catalog.py.
deflator_2025_to_2024.verification_note: Index values from deflator_2023_to_2024's verification_note (BLS API v2 CUUR0000SA0, startyear=2023, endyear=2025: 2024 = 313.689, 2025 = 321.943); 313.689 / 321.943 = 0.9743619 recomputed.

transmission_line_230kv_usd_per_km.units: USD/km (2025 PTO cost-guide dollars; see note)
transmission_line_230kv_usd_per_km.source: PG&E, '2025 PG&E Proposed Generator Interconnection Unit Cost Guide' (Final, posted by CAISO; Cost Details tab, revised 2025-02-24), New HV Transmission Line, 230 kV, Double Circuit strung on both sides, Lattice Tower
transmission_line_230kv_usd_per_km.note: Cost Details row 124 (all costs $x1,000): 'Double Circuit, Strung on both sides, Lattice Tower | per mile | 3392 (60/70 kV) | 3392 (115 kV) | 4007 (230 kV) | N/A (500 kV)'. $4,007,000/mile / 1.609344 km/mile = $2,489,834/km. Configuration: double circuit (two 230 kV circuits on one tower line), chosen so the line can carry about 1 GW with N-1 redundancy. Terrain and length: the guide's base case is 'flat land/rural setting' with line length >=10 miles (factor 1X). Add-on factors are 'hilly (1.2X), mountainous (1.3X), and forested (1.5X)', 'suburban (1.2X) or urban (1.5X)', and line length '<=4 miles (2X), 5 to 9 miles (1.5X - 1.1X)'. Caution: PG&E's own 'Factors and Assumptions' tab gives different terrain multipliers (flat 1, hilly 1.3, mountain 1.5) from this cost-row note. The guide does not state a conductor. For comparison, SCE's 2025 guide gives 220 kV single-circuit lattice towers 'strung with 2B-1590kcmil ACSR conductor'. Scope: 'engineering and construction costs only. Environmental, Permitting, and Right of way Acquisition costs are not included.' Unit costs include 35% contingency ('Contingency factor for New Transmission Line: 35%') and exclude corporate overheads (A&G, P&B, AFUDC), ITCC and environmental monitoring and mitigation. The guide also lists an 'Owner's Representative Fee for EPC construction: 10% of the total project cost'. Other PG&E 230 kV options in $/mile: DC lattice strung one side 3,146k; single-circuit lattice 2,509k ($1,559,020/km); DC tubular steel pole 4,505k ($2,799,277/km). SCE 2025 (2025 constant dollars) gives 220 kV DC lattice 7,263k/mile ($4,513,019/km), so the spread between utilities is about 1.8x. Dollar year: PG&E does not state it on the cost rows. Its 'Escalation Rates & Factors' tab is carried over unchanged from the 2023 guide and still reads 'in 2023 Constant Dollars', but the rows were re-priced: the same row was 3,626k/mile in PG&E's 2023 Final guide. Treat it as 2025 USD, like SCE's 2025 guide, which explicitly says '2025 Constant Dollars'. To get 2024 USD, multiply by 0.974362 (CPI-U, see deflator note).
transmission_line_230kv_usd_per_km.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): re-downloaded pge-2025-per-unit-cost-guide-final.xlsx from caiso.com (byte-identical to the raw copy). Cost Details tab: I1 'All costs are $x1,000', A3 'Revised as of: 2025-02-24', C124 'Double Circuit, Strung on both sides, Lattice Tower', G124 'per mile', K124 (230 kV) = 4007; N124 text as quoted; K125 3146, K126 2509, K127 4505. 4,007,000 / 1.609344 = 2,489,834.4 /km. Newer edition: CAISO's 'Current cost guides' library (checked 2026-10-23) lists only the nine 2025 Final guides (posted 07/15/2025); 2026 guide URLs return 404, so 2025 is current. Dollar year: the 'Escalation Rates & Factors' tab is cell-for-cell identical to the 2023 Final guide (PGAE-2023-Final-Per-Unit-Cost-Guide.xlsx, whose 230 kV DC lattice row is 3626), so the 2023-constant-dollar label is stale; treating the rows as 2025 USD is a judgment call. SCE L95 = 7263 confirmed.

transmission_line_500kv_usd_per_km.source: SCE, '2025 Proposed SCE Generator Interconnection Unit Cost Guide' (Final, posted by CAISO; Cost Details tab, revised 2025-02-19), New HV Transmission Line, 500 kV, Single Circuit, Lattice Tower
transmission_line_500kv_usd_per_km.note: PG&E publishes no 500 kV line cost: '500kV estimates are not provided since PG&E did not build 500kV lines in recent years' (PG&E 2025 guide, row 124). SCE is the next CAISO participating TO. SCE Cost Details row 97 (costs $x1,000): 'Single Circuit, Lattice Tower | per mile | ... | 4865 (230 kV) | 6692 (500 kV)'. $6,692,000/mile / 1.609344 = $4,158,216/km. Configuration: one 500 kV circuit, which can carry about 1 GW on its own; a double circuit would be needed only for N-1 redundancy on a 500 kV gen-tie. Other SCE 500 kV options in $/mile: DC lattice strung both sides 14,866k ($9,237,304/km); DC lattice strung one side 13,429k; single-circuit tubular steel pole 8,387k ($5,211,440/km). Terrain: the base is 'flat land/rural setting'. SCE's factors are higher than PG&E's: 'hilly (1.5X), mountainous (2.0X), and forested (3.0X)', 'suburban (2.0X) or urban (3.0X)', and a weather-loading factor of 1.35X to 1.60X. The guide does not state a 500 kV conductor. Dollar year: 'Current SCE Unit Cost Guide as posted on the CAISO website is in 2025 Constant Dollars' (Escalation tab). Includes 35% contingency. Excludes ROW and easements, environmental work, licensing, permitting, corporate overheads and AFUDC, and ITCC. Caution: SCE's 230 kV unit costs run about 1.8x PG&E's (row 95: 7,263k vs 4,007k/mile), so comparing this 500 kV tier with the PG&E 230 kV tier mixes utility cost levels. To get 2024 USD, multiply by 0.974362.
transmission_line_500kv_usd_per_km.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): sce-2025-per-unit-cost-guide-final.xlsx (byte-identical to the raw copy), Cost Details: A3/F3 revised 2025-02-19; C97 'Single Circuit, Lattice Tower', L97 (230 kV) = 4865, M97 (500 kV) = 6692; M95 14866, M96 13429, M100 8387. Escalation tab B4 'Current SCE Unit Cost Guide as posted on the CAISO website is in 2025 Constant Dollars.'; BulkTrans tab B45 35% contingency, B51 exclusions. PG&E N124 '500kV estimates are not provided since PG&E did not build 500kV lines in recent years.' confirmed. 6,692,000 / 1.609344 = 4,158,216.0 /km.

transmission_line_115kv_usd_per_km.units: USD/km (2025 PTO cost-guide dollars; see 230 kV note)
transmission_line_115kv_usd_per_km.source: PG&E, '2025 PG&E Proposed Generator Interconnection Unit Cost Guide' (Final, posted by CAISO), New HV Transmission Line, 115 kV, Double Circuit strung on both sides, Lattice Tower
transmission_line_115kv_usd_per_km.note: Cost Details row 124: 115 kV column = 3392 ($x1,000 per mile). $3,392,000 / 1.609344 = $2,107,691/km. This uses the same configuration as the 230 kV entry (double circuit, lattice, flat/rural, >=10 miles), so the tiers are like for like. PG&E notes: 'Costs for 60/70kV are same as for 115kV due to same 115kV standards used for new installation or design.' Other PG&E 115 kV options in $/mile: DC tubular steel pole 3,791k ($2,355,618/km); single-circuit TSP 2,349k ($1,459,601/km); wood poles 932k. The same terrain, length and scope factors and dollar-year caveat apply as for the 230 kV entry. A 115 kV double circuit carries only a few hundred MW, far short of a ~1 GW campus.
transmission_line_115kv_usd_per_km.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): PG&E 2025 Final guide, Cost Details J124 (115 kV) = 3392 ($x1,000/mile); J127 3791, J129 2349, J130 932; the N124 60/70 kV sentence is as quoted. 3,392,000 / 1.609344 = 2,107,691.1 /km.

substation_230kv_usd.units: USD per new substation (2025 PTO cost-guide dollars; see 230 kV line note)
substation_230kv_usd.source: PG&E, '2025 PG&E Proposed Generator Interconnection Unit Cost Guide' (Final, posted by CAISO), New Substation Equipment, 'Complete loop-in Substation ... loop in and out two existing PG&E T lines', 230 kV
substation_230kv_usd.note: Cost Details rows 10-12 (costs $x1,000): 'Complete loop-in Substation, equipped with one line position to terminate a single gen-tie and loop in and out two existing PG&E T lines. 2 complete Bays and 1 Partial Bay - 8 CBs | N/A (60/70 kV) | 20000 (115 kV) | 23000 (230 kV) | 65000 (500 kV)'. Configuration: breaker-and-a-half (BAAH), 8 circuit breakers, one gen-tie line position plus two looped-in lines. Scope, quoted: 'Includes all necessary equipment, including operating buses, one double-breaker line position on a breaker-and-a-half (BAAH) configuration for gen-tie, one three-breaker line position on a BAAH configuration to loop each existing transmission line, substation MPAC or control building, and associated protective relays. Also includes base costs of site preparation, ground grid, fencing, driveway and access road (up to .5 mi.) outside substation.' We use the 8-CB layout because it is the only one PG&E prices at 500 kV, which keeps the 230 and 500 kV tiers like for like. The smaller layout (rows 6-8: loop in one line, '1 complete Bay and 1 Partial Bay - 5 CBs') is $19,000k at 230 kV ($16,000k at 115 kV). Adding a BAAH gen-tie position costs $6,000k (2 CB) or $7,200k (3 CB) at 230 kV (rows 36-37), for example for a second gen-tie circuit. Substation contingency is 0%. Excludes land ('Actual'), licensing and permitting, corporate overheads and AFUDC, and ITCC. Cross-check: SCE 2025 (2025$) prices a 230 kV loop-in (BAAH gen-tie position plus loop of one line) at $32,010k. Dollar-year caveat: as for the 230 kV line. In PG&E's 2023 guide the 8-CB 230 kV figure was 22000.
substation_230kv_usd.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): PG&E 2025 Final guide, Cost Details C10-C12 text as quoted ('2 complete Bays and 1 Partial Bay - 8 CBs'), K10 (230 kV) = 23000 ($x1,000); K6 = 19000 and J6 = 16000 (5-CB layout); K36 = 6000 (BAAH 2CB), K37 = 7200 (BAAH 3CB); N6 scope text; Factors tab B42 'Contingency factor for Substation Equipment and Installation: 0% (zero %)'; row 163 land 'Actual'. SCE 2025 L6 = 32,009.98 ($x1,000). PG&E 2023 Final guide L10 (230 kV) = 22000.

substation_500kv_usd.units: USD per new substation (2025 PTO cost-guide dollars; see 230 kV line note)
substation_500kv_usd.source: PG&E, '2025 PG&E Proposed Generator Interconnection Unit Cost Guide' (Final, posted by CAISO), New Substation Equipment, 'Complete loop-in Substation ... loop in and out two existing PG&E T lines', 500 kV; derivation on the 'Other Documentation' tab
substation_500kv_usd.note: Cost Details row 10, 500 kV column = 65000 ($x1,000). This is the same BAAH, 8-CB, two-bay-plus-partial-bay layout as substation_230kv_usd. Caveat: it is a rough PG&E estimate, not built-project data. From the 'Other Documentation' tab: 'PG&E does not have an actual estimate for a new loop-in substation at the 500 kV level since PG&E has not built a 500 kV Sw Sta in years.' PG&E started from 'the 230 kV unit cost of $20M for the same BAAH layout' (an older figure; the 2025 row shows $23M) and doubled it for equipment size and footprint ('$40M'), added impervious security walls with active monitoring (the text says 'a $10M adder' but tallies it as '+$15M') and added relay sets C and D with physical separation ('+$10M'), for '$65M'. The Factors tab adds: 'Installations at 500 kV are rare for generation interconnection projects in PG&E's service area and good cost data is not available.' Cross-check: SCE 2025 (2025 constant dollars) prices a 500 kV complete loop-in substation (BAAH gen-tie position plus loop of one line) at $57,268k, row 6. Excludes land, licensing and permitting, telecom, overheads, AFUDC and ITCC.
substation_500kv_usd.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): PG&E 2025 Final guide, Cost Details L10 (500 kV) = 65000 ($x1,000); 'Other Documentation' tab A1 and 'Factors and Assumptions' B51 texts confirmed. Corrected the note: PG&E's derivation starts from $20M (not the current $23M), and the source's security item is internally inconsistent ($10M vs +$15M). SCE 2025 M6 = 57,268.07 ($x1,000) confirmed.

interconnection_lifetime_years.source: PG&E 2027 General Rate Case (CPUC A.25-05-009), Exhibit PG&E-10, Results of Operations workpapers supporting Chapter 9 Depreciation Study (Errata II, redline, Apr 16 2025): Electric Transmission, FERC Accounts 353.01, 354, 356
interconnection_lifetime_years.note: PG&E's survivor curves (Iowa curve: average service life in years, then dispersion type) for transmission plant. Account 353.01 Station Equipment: 'The 47-R2 survivor curve is the currently authorized curve from the previous GRC' and 'The recommendation is to use the 47-R2 survivor curve' (PDF pp. 414-415, WP 9-408). Account 354 Towers and Fixtures: 'continue to use the 75-R4 survivor curve' (PDF p. 445). Account 356 Overhead Conductors and Devices: 'retain the 65-R1.5 survivor curve' (PDF p. 474). Also from the curve tables: 355 Poles and Fixtures IOWA 56-R1.5 (PDF p. 460), 352 Structures and Improvements IOWA 70-R3 (PDF p. 399). We use one lifetime for the whole interconnection, both line and substation. We pick 47 years, the shortest major component (station equipment), because a shorter life gives less end-of-horizon salvage credit and so errs toward higher cost. Line-only assets would justify 65-75 years. PG&E's narrative notes 'industry expects physical lives of transformers to be around 50 years and ... circuit breakers to be around 40 years'. These are PG&E's book-depreciation parameters; the curves for 353.01 and 354 are the ones currently authorized.
interconnection_lifetime_years.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): downloaded the CPUC-hosted PDF (560 pp.; cover: Application 25-05-009, Exhibit PG&E-10, April 16, 2025, Results of Operations workpapers supporting Errata II testimony, Chapter 9 Part 1 Volume 4 of 8, redline). PDF p. 414 (WP 9-408), Account 353.01: 'The 47-R2 survivor curve is the currently authorized curve from the previous GRC'; p. 415: 'The recommendation is to use the 47-R2 survivor curve'; p. 445, Account 354: 'continue to use the 75-R4 survivor curve'; p. 474, Account 356: 'retain the 65-R1.5 survivor curve'; p. 414 transformer/breaker quote confirmed. The value 47 is a judgment pick (shortest major component), not a single published interconnection life.

land_acres_per_mw_solar_pv.source: Bolinger, M. & Bolinger, G. (2022), 'Land Requirements for Utility-Scale PV: An Empirical Update on Power and Energy Density', IEEE Journal of Photovoltaics, doi:10.1109/JPHOTOV.2021.3136805 (LBNL; author copy hosted by DOE)
land_acres_per_mw_solar_pv.note: Paper p. 6: 'we do have the ability to express power density in ac capacity terms as well, given that we know the dc:ac ratio of each plant. We present those numbers here—0.28 MWAC/acre (0.69 MWAC/hectare) for fixed-tilt and 0.18 MWAC/acre (0.45 MWAC/hectare) for tracking plants'. 1 / 0.18 = 5.56 acres/MWac for single-axis tracking, the median for 2019 plants. The DC basis is 0.24 MWdc/acre (4.2 acres/MWdc) for tracking, per the LBNL summary slides (p. 13) 'Power density: 0.35 MWDC/acre (2.8 acres/MWDC) for fixed-tilt and 0.24 MWDC/acre (4.2 acres/MWDC) for tracking', https://emp.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/emp-files/land_requirements_for_utility-scale_pv.pdf. Caveat: this is the direct area occupied by the PV arrays, not the total fenced or leased site. The authors explain that total site boundaries are rarely visible in imagery and that the array-to-site ratio varies widely: for Copper Mountain 3 (345 MWdc / 255 MWac) the array is 945 acres of a 1,375-acre lease (69%). Scaling by that one example would give about 8.1 acres/MWac total, but the paper warns the 69% ratio 'provides little or no information content'. The slides (p. 7) suggest de-rating instead: 'if only 75% of your site is buildable, just multiply our numbers by 75%'. Engineering cross-check for a whole (typically leased) site: EIA/Sargent & Lundy Jan 2024 cost study, Case 16 'Solar PV with Single-Axis Tracking 150 MW AC, DC / AC Ratio 1.3', 'Estimated Land Requirement (Note 1) acres 1000' (PDF p. 140) = 6.67 acres/MWac. The sample is 736 U.S. plants (35.5 GWdc / 27.0 GWac) built 2007-2019. Median tracking density rose 43% from 2011 to 2019, and newer bifacial or larger-format modules may be denser.
land_acres_per_mw_solar_pv.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): DOE-hosted author copy (byte-identical to the raw copy), p. 6: '0.28 MW AC/acre (0.69 MW AC/hectare) for fixed-tilt and 0.18 MW AC/acre (0.45 MW AC/hectare) for tracking plants'; 1 / 0.18 = 5.556 acres/MWac. p. 3: Copper Mountain 3 945 vs 1375 acres, and 736 plants, 35,482 MWDC (27,001 MWAC). LBNL slides p. 13 (DC benchmarks) and p. 7 confirmed; corrected the slide quote to include the DC subscripts. Open definitional issue: this is direct array area per MWac, while the spec asks for total site area. LBNL does not publish a total-site metric; EIA Case 16 (6.67 acres/MWac, leased site) is added as a cross-check.

land_acres_per_mw_onshore_wind.source: Denholm, P., Hand, M., Jackson, M. & Ong, S. (2009), 'Land-Use Requirements of Modern Wind Power Plants in the United States', NREL/TP-6A2-45834, Table 1
land_acres_per_mw_onshore_wind.note: Table 1 'Summary of Collected Wind Power Plant Area Data' (PDF p. 16): 'Average Area Requirements (hectare/MW) | 0.3 ± 0.3 (permanent direct) | 0.7 ± 0.6 (temporary direct) | 34.5 ± 22.4 (total area)'. Total area is a capacity-weighted average over 161 projects (25,438 MW). 34.5 ha/MW x 2.4710538 acres/ha = 85.25 acres/MW (± 55.4 acres/MW). The text adds: 'an overall average capacity density of 3.0 ± 1.7 MW/km2' and '125 (representing 80% of the evaluated capacity) have reported area of between 10 and 50 hectares/MW'. The report separates 'direct impact (i.e., disturbed land due to physical infrastructure development)' from 'total area (i.e., land associated with the complete wind plant project)'. Only the direct area (separate key) is disturbed. The sample is plants >20 MW built after 2000, so modern larger turbines and spacing may differ. NREL is now NLR; the report was fetched from the NLR docs host (also OSTI 964608).
land_acres_per_mw_onshore_wind.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): fetched https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy09osti/45834.pdf (curl works with a browser User-Agent; https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/964608 redirects to the same, byte-identical file). Cover: NREL/TP-6A2-45834, August 2009. PDF p. 16, Table 1: 161 projects, 25,438 MW, 'Average Area Requirements (hectare/MW) 0.3 ± 0.3 | 0.7 ± 0.6 | 34.5 ± 22.4'. PDF p. 20: '3.0 ± 1.7 MW/km2' and the 125-project (80%) sentence. PDF p. 11: sample 'constructed after 2000 and with a nameplate capacity greater than 20 MW'. 34.5 × 2.4710538 = 85.25 acres/MW; 22.4 × 2.4710538 = 55.35.

land_acres_per_mw_onshore_wind_direct.source: Denholm, P., Hand, M., Jackson, M. & Ong, S. (2009), 'Land-Use Requirements of Modern Wind Power Plants in the United States', NREL/TP-6A2-45834, Section 4.2
land_acres_per_mw_onshore_wind_direct.note: PDF p. 18: 'The overall average direct impact area is 0.3 ± 0.3 hectares/MW for permanent impact and 0.7 ± 0.6 hectares/MW for temporary impact, or a total direct surface area disruption of about 1.0 ± 0.7 hectares/MW.' 1.0 ha/MW x 2.4710538 = 2.47 acres/MW. The permanent footprint alone (turbine pads, roads, substation, O&M buildings) is 0.3 ha/MW = 0.74 acres/MW. Temporary impact (laydown areas, temporary roads) is 0.7 ha/MW = 1.73 acres/MW and is mostly restored after construction. Use 0.74 acres/MW if only the long-term disturbed area should count.
land_acres_per_mw_onshore_wind_direct.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): same PDF, p. 18: 'The overall average direct impact area is 0.3 ± 0.3 hectares/MW for permanent impact and 0.7 ± 0.6 hectares/MW for temporary impact, or a total direct surface area disruption of about 1.0 ± 0.7 hectares/MW.' 1.0 × 2.4710538 = 2.47; 0.3 ha = 0.74 acres; 0.7 ha = 1.73 acres.

land_acres_per_mw_gas_cc.source: U.S. EIA (prepared by Sargent & Lundy), 'Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Electric Power Generating Technologies', January 2024 (AEO2025 cost study), Case 5 'CC 2x2x1 H-Class', Table 5-1
land_acres_per_mw_gas_cc.note: Table 5-1, Case 5 Capital Cost Estimate (PDF p. 76): 'Configuration CC 2x2x1 H-Class | Net Plant Capacity (60°F, 60% RH) MW 1227 | Estimated Land Requirement acres 30'. 30 / 1,227 = 0.0245 acres/MW. Case 5 is the closest EIA case to ATB's 'NG 2-on-1 Combined Cycle (H-Frame)'. It is an engineering estimate for a generic greenfield site, not a survey of built plants, hence 'assumption'. Alternatives: EIA Case 6 (CC 1x1x1 single-shaft H-class, 627 MW, 30 acres) = 0.048 acres/MW. NETL's NGCC study (DOE/NETL-2023-3922, Oct 2023, https://www.netl.doe.gov/projects/files/NaturalGasCombinedCycleNGCCPowerPlantswithCarbonCaptureandExhaustGasRecycleEGR_101623.pdf, p. 10) says 'The NGCC plant proper occupies about 10 acres leaving a buffer of 0.24 km (0.15 mi) to the plant fence line for a total area of 100 acres'. For its H-class base case (992 MWe net) that is 0.010 acres/MW for the plant proper and 0.101 acres/MW for the fenced site.
land_acres_per_mw_gas_cc.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): eia.gov capital_cost_AEO2025.pdf (byte-identical; cover 'January 2024'; p. 3 says it was commissioned for AEO2025). PDF p. 76, Table 5-1 Case 5: 'Configuration CC 2x2x1 H-Class', 'Net Plant Capacity (60°F, 60% RH) MW 1227', 'Estimated Land Requirement acres 30', so 30 / 1227 = 0.02445. Case 6: net 627 MW (PDF p. 83) and 30 acres (p. 84), so 0.0478. NETL DOE/NETL-2023-3922 (October 16, 2023), PDF p. 22: 'The NGCC plant proper occupies about 10 acres ... for a total area of 100 acres'; H-class base case net 992 MWe (PDF p. 16).

land_acres_per_mw_gas_ct.source: U.S. EIA (prepared by Sargent & Lundy), 'Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Electric Power Generating Technologies', January 2024 (AEO2025 cost study), Case 4 'CT – Simple Cycle H-Class', Table 4-1
land_acres_per_mw_gas_ct.note: Table 4-1, Case 4 Capital Cost Estimate (PDF p. 69): 'Configuration CT – Simple Cycle H-Class | 1 x 430 MW rating | Net Plant Capacity (60°F, 60% RH) MW 419 | Estimated Land Requirement acres 20'. 20 / 419 = 0.0477 acres/MW. Case 4 is EIA's only heavy-duty frame simple-cycle case; ATB's gas_ct is an F-frame. An F-frame unit is smaller than this H-class unit, so on a similar site its land per MW would be higher. The other simple-cycle case, Case 3 'CT – Simple Cycle 4 x Aeroderivative Class' (211 MW net, 20 acres, PDF p. 63), gives 0.095 acres/MW and serves as an upper reference. It is an engineering estimate for a generic site, hence 'assumption'.
land_acres_per_mw_gas_ct.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): same EIA PDF, p. 69, Table 4-1 Case 4: 'CT – Simple Cycle H-Class ... 1 x 430 MW rating', net plant capacity 419 MW, estimated land requirement 20 acres, so 20 / 419 = 0.0477. PDF p. 63, Case 3 '4 x Aeroderivative Class': 211 MW, 20 acres, so 0.0948.

land_acres_per_mw_battery.source: U.S. EIA (prepared by Sargent & Lundy), 'Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Electric Power Generating Technologies', January 2024 (AEO2025 cost study), Case 19 'Battery Energy Storage System, 150 MW | 600 MWh', Table 19-1
land_acres_per_mw_battery.note: Table 19-1, Case 19 Capital Cost Estimate (PDF p. 157): 'Power Rating MW 150 | Energy Rating MWh 600 | Estimated Land Requirement acres 6'. 6 / 150 = 0.04 acres/MW, or 6 / 600 = 0.01 acres/MWh. The case is a lithium-ion BESS of '240 modular, factory-integrated battery storage containers', each '20 feet long x 10 feet wide x 8 feet high', with inverter-transformer PCS skids and a substation stepping up to 138 kV. EIA says container offerings 'vary in size and modularity but offer roughly the same energy density per acre'. For other durations, scale with energy: acres ≈ 0.01 x MWh. It is an engineering estimate for a generic site, hence 'assumption'.
land_acres_per_mw_battery.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): same EIA PDF, p. 157, Case 19: 'Battery Energy Storage System 150 MW | 600 MWh', 'Estimated Land Requirement acres 6', 'Power Rating MW 150 Energy Rating MWh 600 Duration hour 4'; 6 / 150 = 0.04 and 6 / 600 = 0.01. PDF p. 155 holds the container quotes ('240 modular, factory-integrated battery storage containers', '20 feet long x 10 feet wide x 8 feet high', 'roughly the same energy density per acre') and the 138 kV interconnection.

gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_monthly_usd_.source: CAISO Department of Market Monitoring, '2024 Annual Report on Market Issues and Performance' (Aug 7 2025), Figure 2.7 'Monthly average PG&E Citygate gas price and load-weighted average electricity prices for balancing areas in day-ahead market (CAISO)', with Figure 1.70 as a cross-check
gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_monthly_usd_.note: The planned source was not available. EIA's wholesale page (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/wholesale/) has ICE daily natural-gas hub files only for 2014-2017; the last, xls/archive/ice_natgas-2017final.xlsx, ends on trade date 2017-12-28. The 2018+ files, including ice_electric-2024final.xlsx, cover electricity hubs only. We found no free daily 2024 PG&E Citygate series. Method: DMM's Figure 2.7 (printed p. 128, PDF p. 140) is a vector chart. backend/app/evaluate/prep_gas.py reads the 24 vertices (Jan 2023 to Dec 2024) of the dashed 'PG&E Citygate gas price' polyline from the PDF content stream, picks the line by matching the legend sample's stroke and dash, and converts its y coordinates to $/MMBtu with a least-squares fit of the chart's gridlines to the right-axis ticks ($0 to $16). This list is the last 12 values, rounded to 2 dp. Accuracy: the PDF stores vertices on a 0.8 pt grid, which at 11.34 pt per $/MMBtu gives about ±$0.035 per month. Checks the script enforces: (1) the 12-month mean, 3.0757, must be within 0.03 of DMM's text 'PG&E Citygate gas price ... averaging about $3.08/MMBtu in 2024', which also appears in the Figure 1.70 table ('PG&E Citygate $6.10 (2023) $3.08 (2024)'); (2) the PG&E Citygate line in Figure 1.70 (printed p. 88, coarser axis, ±$0.08) must agree in every 2024 month, and it does to within 0.116 $/MMBtu. The pattern fits DMM's text ('a spike in natural gas prices in January 2024 due to extreme cold weather in the Pacific Northwest over the Martin Luther King Jr. Day weekend') and EIA's weekly spot quotes (Natural Gas Weekly Update, Feb 15 2024, https://www.eia.gov/naturalgas/weekly/archivenew_ngwu/2024/02_15/: 'The price at PG&E Citygate in Northern California fell 62 cents, down from $3.54/MMBtu last Wednesday to $2.92/MMBtu yesterday'). DMM does not name its price vendor in this section. Intended use: monthly shape s_m = p_m / mean(p) applied to the scenario's annual gas price. DMM's 2024 quarterly reports give stated PG&E Citygate quarterly averages of Q1 $3.85, Q2 $2.21, Q3 $2.80 and Q4 $3.48 (Avg Hub Price tables beside Figure 1.1 in each report); this list gives 3.84 / 2.20 / 2.78 / 3.49. Independent daily cross-check (verifier, 2026-10-23): CAISO OASIS PRC_FUEL daily price for fuel region FRPGE2 (https://oasis.caiso.com/oasisapi/SingleZip?queryname=PRC_FUEL&fuel_region_id=FRPGE2 ...). CAISO's fuelregion_electricregiondefinitions.xlsx defines FRPGE2 as pricing hub 'PG&E Citygate' + 'PG&E Schedule G-EG -All Other' transport, with no shrinkage and no GHG adder. OPR_DT is the gas flow day. The cross-check subtracts a piecewise-constant transport offset for each tariff period. The periods were found from steps in FRPGE1 − 1.0167·FRPGE2. Each offset is the median of FRPGE2(flow day) − the EIA Natural Gas Weekly Update Wednesday PG&E Citygate quote (trade day), over 48 Wednesdays: $2.58 Jan 1-17, $3.84 Jan 18-Mar 13, $3.92 Mar 14-Apr 16, $4.02 Apr 17-Sep 24, $4.66 Sep 25-Dec 31. The spread within each period is ±$0.017. This gives 2024 flow-day monthly means [6.17, 2.98, 2.46, 2.27, 2.24, 2.15, 3.12, 2.73, 2.53, 3.84, 3.14, 3.40] (mean of months 3.085). That agrees with the DMM list within ±0.09 in 10 of 12 months. The reconstruction is 0.26 lower in October and 0.17 higher in November, while the Q4 means agree (3.46 vs 3.49). DMM's SoCal Citygate line shows the same October (+0.26) and November (−0.14) offsets against an identical reconstruction for SoCal (fuel region FRSCE3 vs EIA weekly SoCal quotes). The difference therefore comes from how DMM buckets or weights months, not from reading the chart. Monthly shape factors p_m/mean(p) differ by at most 0.088 (October: 1.332 DMM vs 1.244 reconstructed). Verifier raw files: data/evaluate/raw/costs_verify/oasis_prc_fuel/, ngwu/.
gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_monthly_usd_.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): re-downloaded the DMM PDF (byte-identical to the raw copy) and re-ran prep_gas.py. Its output matches this list exactly (12-month mean 3.0757, day-weighted 3.0828, Fig 1.70 max diff 0.116, checks passed). Hub, units and dates: the line is the legend series 'PG&E Citygate gas price', plotted on the right axis 'Gas price ($/MMBtu)' ($0-$16), with 24 monthly vertices Jan 2023-Dec 2024 under month labels; the last 12 are calendar 2024. DMM does not say whether its months use trade or flow dates. The values faithfully reproduce the cited DMM figure and DMM's stated quarterly averages (each within $0.02). The independent daily cross-check (CAISO OASIS FRPGE2 anchored to 48 EIA weekly quotes) agrees within ±0.09 except October (DMM +0.26) and November (DMM −0.17); see the note. ICE daily gas files on EIA's wholesale page stop at 2017 (ice_natgas-2017final.xlsx: last trade date 2017-12-28, includes 'PG&E - Citygate'); 2018+ and 2024 gas file names redirect to eia.gov/electricity/.

gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_avg_usd_per_.source: Mean of gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_monthly_usd_per_mmbtu (CAISO DMM 2024 Annual Report, Figure 2.7, read by backend/app/evaluate/prep_gas.py); matches DMM's stated 2024 average
gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_avg_usd_per_.note: Simple mean of the 12 unrounded monthly values = 3.0757, which rounds to 3.08; the mean of the rounded list is 3.075. DMM publishes only monthly averages, so a trade-day-weighted mean cannot be computed from this source. The verifier's daily reconstruction (CAISO OASIS FRPGE2 anchored to EIA weekly quotes; see the monthly entry) gives a trade-date-weighted 2024 mean of about 3.10 $/MMBtu (one value per trade date, with weekend and holiday packages counted once; 256 trade dates, approximate), a calendar flow-day mean of 3.09 and a mean of months of 3.085. The calendar-day-weighted mean (366 days in 2024) is 3.0828 $/MMBtu. DMM states the same figure directly (printed p. 128): 'PG&E Citygate gas price has remained down after declining from January 2023, averaging about $3.08/MMBtu in 2024.' For comparison, the EIA California citygate annual average for 2024 is 3.65 $/MMBtu (see eia_citygate_ca_2024_avg_usd_per_mmbtu). That is a volume-weighted price paid by local distribution companies, not a hub spot price.
gas_price_pge_citygate_2024_avg_usd_per_.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): DMM 2024 annual report, printed p. 128 (PDF p. 140): 'PG&E Citygate gas price has remained down after declining from January 2023, averaging about $3.08/MMBtu in 2024.' The Figure 1.70 table (PDF p. 100) reads 'PG&E Citygate $6.10 $3.08' (2023, 2024). The mean of the 12 unrounded monthly values is 3.0757, which rounds to 3.08. The independent daily reconstruction gives 3.085 to 3.10, depending on weighting.

eia_citygate_ca_2024_avg_usd_per_mmbtu.source: U.S. EIA, 'Natural Gas Citygate Price in California (Dollars per Thousand Cubic Feet)', annual, series N3050CA3 (EIA API v2 id NG.N3050CA3.A); heat content from EIA 'Heat Content of Natural Gas Delivered to Consumers' (Btu per cubic foot), California
eia_citygate_ca_2024_avg_usd_per_mmbtu.note: EIA annual table, decade row quoted: '2020's 3.02 4.29 8.02 8.69 3.79 NA' (2020 to 2025), so 2024 = 3.79 $/Mcf (release date 9/30/2026). The downloaded XLS (https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/hist_xls/N3050CA3a.xls) shows 'Sourcekey N3050CA3'. Conversion: EIA heat content of gas delivered to consumers, California, 2020-2025 row 'California 1,033 1,034 1,035 1,034 1,038 1,022' (https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/ng_cons_heat_a_EPG0_VGTH_btucf_a.htm), so 2024 = 1,038 Btu/cf = 1.038 MMBtu/Mcf. 3.79 / 1.038 = 3.651 $/MMBtu. The 2024 monthly series N3050CA3 (https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/hist_xls/N3050CA3m.xls), in $/Mcf: Jan 4.35, Feb 5.59, Mar 4.23, Apr 2.66, May 2.51, Jun 2.50, Jul 2.98, Aug 3.14, Sep 2.44, Oct 3.22, Nov 3.74, Dec 4.68. For gas sold to electric power consumers in California (series N3045CA3, $/Mcf, 2024): Jan 6.69, Feb 4.23, Mar 3.17, Apr 3.07, May 2.98, Jun 3.16, Jul 3.54, Aug 3.29, Sep 2.97, Oct 3.89, Nov 3.75, Dec 4.25. Citygate is the price at which local distribution companies receive gas, including commodity and interstate transport. It is higher than the PG&E Citygate hub spot average (3.08). It is a candidate default for assumptions.gas_price_usd_per_mmbtu if the contract default changes.
eia_citygate_ca_2024_avg_usd_per_mmbtu.verification_note: Verified 2026-10-23 (verifier): eia.gov/dnav/ng/hist/n3050ca3a.htm 'Natural Gas Citygate Price in California (Dollars per Thousand Cubic Feet)', row 2020's '3.02 4.29 8.02 8.69 3.79 NA', Release Date 9/30/2026. EIA API v2 /seriesid/NG.N3050CA3.A returns 2024 = 3.79 $/MCF, series N3050CA3. The XLS shows Sourcekey N3050CA3. On the heat content page, California 2020-2025 = '1,033 1,034 1,035 1,034 1,038 1,022' Btu/cf, so 3.79 / 1.038 = 3.6513, rounded to 3.65. The 2024 monthly rows of N3050CA3 and N3045CA3 (hist/n3050ca3m.htm, n3045ca3m.htm) match the note.
